assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 60,000 queries/s at peak. Note the unit: this is KEYSTROKES, not searches — a user typing an eight-character query issues five or six requests. Client-side debouncing (150-250 ms) is what keeps this number from being three times larger, and it is a client decision this model cannot see.

assumptions.subject: cdn
assumptions.statement: Prefix popularity is extremely skewed, so ~40% of keystrokes are answered at the edge and never reach the origin at all (the 'edge_hit' flow terminates at the CDN). That skew is the single biggest lever in this design: if personalised suggestions defeat edge caching, origin load nearly doubles overnight.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: An 80% Redis hit rate on prefix -> top-K (trie visit_prob 0.2). Head prefixes are cached; the tail falls through to the index shards.

assumptions.subject: trie
assumptions.statement: The suggestion index is a trie/FST held ENTIRELY IN RAM and sharded by prefix range — memory-class instances are chosen for that reason, not for CPU. The engine sizes this tier by rps only; it has no memory model, so it cannot tell you when the index outgrows the box, which is the actual failure mode.

assumptions.subject: latency
assumptions.statement: The requirement typeahead is really judged on is a p99 UNDER ~100 ms, because a suggestion that arrives after the next keystroke is wasted work. Read this design's latency output as the constraint and the throughput as secondary — the reverse of most systems in this library.

assumptions.subject: index_refresh
assumptions.statement: Index building is genuinely an OFFLINE batch job (mine query logs, rebuild the FST, ship it to the shards). It is modelled here as a thin 1% request flow purely so the term store and the shard-push path are not orphaned components; do not read 600 rps as a real refresh rate.

assumptions.subject: quality
assumptions.statement: Ranking quality — typo tolerance, fuzzy matching, personalisation, freshness — is what makes typeahead good and is entirely outside a capacity model. Fuzzy/edit-distance matching in particular costs far more per query than the flat per-shard rate assumed here.

_library.summary: Every keystroke answered in under 100 ms from an edge cache, a prefix cache, then in-memory index shards.
